nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the New England village sketch
literary_identity: Poet and story-writer; the first American writer to record the New England village in its own dialect and its own harshness.
biography: Born Rose Terry in West Hartford, Connecticut, on 17 February 1827; she taught school, wrote for the Atlantic Monthly from its first number, and published Poems (1860), Happy Dodd (1878), Somebody's Neighbors (1881) and Root-Bound (1885). She married Rollin Cooke in 1873 and died at Pittsfield, Massachusetts, on 18 July 1892.
literary_profile: Rose Terry Cooke was the first American writer to record the New England village in its own dialect and its own harshness, and her stories of the declining farm and the spinster are the finest of the local-colour tales of the 1870s and 1880s. She prepared the way for Mary E. Wilkins Freeman and Sarah Orne Jewett.
stylistic_characteristics: The dialect story of the Connecticut farm; the spinster and the hired girl as central figures; the grim detail and the refusal of sentiment; the sketch without a plot; the old-time frame of the grandmother's memory.
intellectual_concerns: The vanishing New England farm; poverty and the woman's lot; the Calvinist inheritance and its repression; regional identity and the decay of the village; age and solitude.
historical_significance: Rose Terry Cooke was the first American writer to record the New England village in its own dialect and its own harshness: her stories of the declining farm and the spinster are the finest local-colour tales of the period and prepared the way for Mary E. Wilkins Freeman and Sarah Orne Jewett.

literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the first writer to make the Southern mountaineer a subject of American literature.
biography: Born Mary Noailles Murfree at Murfreesboro, Tennessee, on 24 January 1850; lame from childhood, she spent her summers in the mountains of east Tennessee and published In the Tennessee Mountains under the name Charles Egbert Craddock in 1884. The Prophet of the Great Smoky Mountains (1885), The Despot of Broomsedge Cove (1889) and The Frontiersmen (1904) followed. She died at Murfreesboro on 31 July 1922.
literary_profile: Mary Noailles Murfree was the first writer to make the Southern mountaineer a subject of American literature: her Tennessee mountain stories of 1884 created the genre, and her dialect, her landscape and her feud narratives prepared the way for the Southern Renaissance and for the Appalachian novel.
stylistic_characteristics: The mountain dialect rendered phonetically; the landscape of the Great Smokies as a character; the feud and the clan; the frame of the outsider visitor; the tragic ending without consolation.
intellectual_concerns: Regional identity and the American sectional character; the mountain poor and the feud; isolation and the closed community; the closing of the American frontier; the Southern past.
historical_significance: Mary Noailles Murfree was the first writer to make the Southern mountaineer a subject of American literature: her Tennessee mountain stories created the genre, and her dialect, landscape and feud narratives prepared the way for the Southern Renaissance.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Louisiana story and the Creole memory
literary_identity: Novelist and historian; the finest writer of the Louisiana local-colour story and the recorder of the Creole past.
biography: Born Grace Elizabeth King in New Orleans on 29 November 1852; after the failure of her family's sugar plantation she turned to writing, and Balcony Stories (1893) made her reputation. Monsieur Motte (1888), Tales of a Time and Place (1892), New Orleans: The Place and the People (1895) and The Pleasant Ways of St Medard (1916) followed. She died in New Orleans on 14 January 1932.
literary_profile: Grace King was the finest writer of the Louisiana local-colour story and the recorder of the Creole past: Balcony Stories is one of the great American story collections of the century, and her work gave the New Orleans of the old regime its literary monument and challenged the Northern version of Reconstruction.
stylistic_characteristics: The balcony story told from above the street; the Creole French in direct speech; the elegiac frame of the lost regime; the ironic ending; the history folded into anecdote.
intellectual_concerns: The Southern past and the burden of history; race, the colour line and Reconstruction; the Creole inheritance; poverty and the fallen family; the city and the old quarter.
historical_significance: Grace King was the finest writer of the Louisiana local-colour story and the recorder of the Creole past: Balcony Stories is one of the great American story collections of the century, and her work gave New Orleans its literary monument.

literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the author of The Morgesons, one of the strangest and most original American novels of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born Elizabeth Drew Barstow in Mattapoisett, Massachusetts, on 6 May 1823; she married the poet Richard Henry Stoddard in 1851 and moved to New York, where she wrote for the magazines. The Morgesons (1862), Two Men (1865) and Temple House (1867) followed, with Poems (1895). She died in New York on 1 August 1902.
literary_profile: Elizabeth Stoddard wrote The Morgesons, one of the strangest and most original American novels of the nineteenth century and a direct ancestor of the modern novel of female desire: her heroines' refusal of the marriage plot and her abrupt, dislocated style made her a writer rediscovered by feminist criticism and now recognised as a major American novelist.
stylistic_characteristics: The abrupt, unassimilated scene; the refusal of narrative explanation; the heroine's erotic and economic self-interest; the grotesque minor character; the New England town as a closed system.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question and the limited estate; female desire and its punishment; the New England town and its hypocrisies; money and marriage; the failure of the family.
historical_significance: Elizabeth Stoddard wrote The Morgesons, one of the most original American novels of the century and a direct ancestor of the modern novel of female desire: rediscovered by feminist criticism, she is now recognised as a major American novelist.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Great Lakes story and the European exile
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest American regionalist of the 1870s and the close friend of Henry James.
biography: Born Constance Fenimore Woolson at Claremont, New Hampshire, on 5 March 1840, a great-niece of James Fenimore Cooper; she grew up in Cleveland, published Castle Nowhere (1875) and Rodman the Keeper (1880), and lived in Europe from 1879. Anne (1882), For the Major (1883) and Jupiter Lights (1889) followed. She died in Venice on 24 January 1894.
literary_profile: Constance Fenimore Woolson was the finest American regionalist of the 1870s and the closest American friend of Henry James: her Great Lakes and Southern stories created the American regional tale at its most finished, and her European novels made the American woman abroad into a subject of the first importance.
stylistic_characteristics: The regional sketch of the Great Lakes and the Sea Islands; the precise topography and the social detail; the American woman abroad; the ironic ending and the withheld marriage; the Jamesian point of view.
intellectual_concerns: Regional identity and the American sectional character; the woman alone and the limited estate; the American in Europe and the expatriate; the Reconstruction South; art and the woman artist.
historical_significance: Constance Fenimore Woolson was the finest American regionalist of the 1870s and Henry James's closest American friend: her Great Lakes and Southern stories created the American regional tale at its most finished, and her European novels made the American woman abroad a subject of the first importance.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Indian rights advocate and the California romance
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and reformer; the author of A Century of Dishonor and Ramona, the most influential American novel about the Native American.
biography: Born Helen Maria Fiske at Amherst, Massachusetts, on 15 October 1830; after the deaths of her husband and two sons she turned to writing, publishing Verses (1870), Bits of Travel (1872) and Saxe Holm's Stories (1874). A Century of Dishonor (1881) and Ramona (1884) made her the leading advocate of Indian rights. She died in San Francisco on 12 August 1885.
literary_profile: Helen Hunt Jackson wrote the two most influential books of the American Indian rights movement: A Century of Dishonor is the founding documentary indictment of American policy, and Ramona is the most widely read American novel about the Native American and the founding text of the California romance.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary record of treaties and massacres; the romance of the California mission; the sentimental heroine as political argument; the landscape of Southern California; the direct appeal to the reader's conscience.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction; race, voice, and the dialect of freedom; the American wilderness and the myth of the forest; the closing of the American frontier.
historical_significance: Helen Hunt Jackson wrote the two most influential books of the American Indian rights movement: A Century of Dishonor is the founding documentary indictment of American policy, and Ramona is the most widely read American novel about the Native American.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the abolitionist colonel and the man of letters
literary_identity: Minister, abolitionist, soldier and man of letters; the colonel of the first Black regiment in the Union army and the correspondent of Emily Dickinson.
biography: Born in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 22 December 1823; he was a Unitarian minister, a leading abolitionist, and the colonel of the 1st South Carolina Volunteers, the first Black regiment in the Union army. Army Life in a Black Regiment (1870), Common Sense about Women (1881) and his editions of Margaret Fuller and Emily Dickinson followed. He died in Cambridge on 9 May 1911.
literary_profile: Thomas Wentworth Higginson was the colonel of the first Black regiment in the Union army and one of the great American abolitionists: Army Life in a Black Regiment is the finest firsthand record of the Black soldier in the Civil War, and his correspondence with Emily Dickinson makes him a central figure in the history of American poetry.
stylistic_characteristics: The regimental memoir of the camp and the march; the transcribed spirituals and the dialect; the abolitionist argument in the essay; the editorial intervention in the poet's text; the plain, energetic, reformist prose.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction; race, voice, and the dialect of freedom; the American experiment and democracy; the woman question; the education of the self.
historical_significance: Thomas Wentworth Higginson was the colonel of the first Black regiment in the Union army: Army Life in a Black Regiment is the finest firsthand record of the Black soldier in the Civil War, and his correspondence with Emily Dickinson makes him central to the history of American poetry.

literary_identity: Journalist and novelist; the author of Looking Backward, the most influential American utopia ever written.
biography: Born in Chicopee Falls, Massachusetts, on 26 March 1850; he studied law, turned to journalism, and published Six to One (1878), Dr Heidenhoff's Process (1880) and Miss Ludington's Sister (1884) before Looking Backward (1888) made him famous. Equality (1897) followed, and he edited the New Nation until his death in Chicopee Falls on 22 May 1898.
literary_profile: Edward Bellamy wrote the most influential American utopia ever written: Looking Backward sold in the hundreds of thousands, founded the Nationalist movement, and created the mass readership for the socialist future; it is the founding text of the American utopian novel and one of the most read books of the nineteenth century.
stylistic_characteristics: The sleeper-awakes frame; the guided tour of the future society; the documentary exposition of the new economy; the romance that crosses the centuries; the plain, expository, persuasive prose of the reformer.
intellectual_concerns: Money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment; wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; the machine age, speed, and technical modernity.
historical_significance: Edward Bellamy wrote the most influential American utopia ever written: Looking Backward sold in the hundreds of thousands, founded the Nationalist movement, and created the mass readership for the socialist future, making it one of the most widely read books of the nineteenth century.
